title: Data Storage and Operations

toc.title: Database Processing Types: ACID, BASE, CAP

html:
1Definition and Goals

Definition: The design, implementation, and support of stored data to maximize its value throughout its lifecycle (from creation/acquisition to disposal).

Two Sub-Activities:

  1. Database Support — data lifecycle activities (implementation, backup, purge, performance)
  2. Database Technology Support — technical requirements, architecture, installing/administering technology

3 Goals:

  1. Manage availability of data throughout the data lifecycle
  2. Ensure the integrity of data assets
  3. Manage the performance of data transactions

Primary Business Driver: Business continuity — if a system becomes unavailable, operations may stop.

2Guiding Principles

DBAs follow 5 guiding principles:

  1. Identify and act on automation opportunities — automate development processes, shorten cycles
  2. Build with reuse in mind — abstracted/reusable data objects prevent tight coupling
  3. Understand and appropriately apply best practices — flexible, not dogmatic
  4. Connect database standards to support requirements — SLA reflects DBA-recommended methods
  5. Set expectations for the DBA role in project work — onboard DBA in project definition phase

3Key Personnel: DBA Types

DBA = most established and most widely adopted data professional role

DBA Type Primary Responsibility
Production DBA Data operations: performance, backup/recovery, clustering/failover, archiving
Application DBA One or more databases in ALL environments (dev/test/QA/prod)
Procedural DBA Stored procedures, triggers, user-defined functions (UDFs)
Development DBA Data design, sandbox/exploration environments
NSA (Network Storage Administrator) Hardware/software supporting data storage arrays

Procedural and Development DBA functions are often combined in one position.

DBA as Level 2 technical support — works with help desks and vendor support.

4Database Architecture Types

Centralized vs. Distributed

  • Centralized — all data in one system; single point of failure risk
  • Distributed — multiple databases on multiple systems; uses commodity hardware; designed to scale out; software replicates data for high availability

MapReduce — computational paradigm used by some distributed databases; divides data request into many small fragments; data co-located on compute nodes.

Federated Databases

  • Provisions data without additional persistence or duplication of source data
  • Maps multiple autonomous database systems into a single federated database
  • No actual data integration — data interoperability manages the view
  • Alternative to merging disparate databases
  • Best for: heterogeneous and distributed integration, enterprise information integration, data virtualization, schema matching, MDM

Two coupling types:

Type Description
Loosely Coupled Component DBs construct own federated schema; user needs direct knowledge of federated schema
Tightly Coupled Independent processes construct/publish integrated federated schema; same schema applies to all; no data replication

Blockchain Database

  • Type of federated database for secure financial transactions (also: contracts, health information)
  • Two structure types: individual records and blocks
  • Each block contains information from the previous block (chain)
  • Hash algorithms create block information
  • Once new block created, old block hash never changes (immutable)
  • Tampering is apparent when hash values no longer match

Virtualization / Cloud Platforms

Three implementation methods:

  1. Virtual Machine Image — run DB on VM instance
  2. Database-as-a-Service (DaaS) — no VM; provider installs/maintains; pay per usage
  3. Managed Database Hosting — cloud hosts and manages on application owner's behalf

4 cloud integration concerns: Standardization/consolidation, Server virtualization, Automation, Security

5Database Processing Types: ACID, BASE, CAP

ACID

  • Coined: Haerder and Reuter (1983) — Jim Gray established the concept
  • Purpose: Indispensable constraint for reliability in database transactions (since early 1980s)
  • Dominant in relational database storage; most use SQL
Letter Meaning
A — Atomicity All operations perform, or none do
C — Consistency Transaction must meet all rules; no half-completed transactions
I — Isolation Each transaction is independent
D — Durability Once complete, cannot be undone

BASE

  • Arose from: unprecedented increase in data volumes/variability; need for unstructured data, read-optimized workloads, flexibility in scaling
  • Common in Big Data environments; used by large online organizations and social media
Letter Meaning
B — Basically Available System guarantees some availability even with node failures; data may be stale
S — Soft State Data in constant flux; not guaranteed to be current
E — Eventual Consistency Data will eventually be consistent across all nodes, but not at every moment

ACID vs BASE Summary Table

Item ACID BASE
Data Structure Schema must exist (schema on write) Dynamic (schema on read)
Consistency Strong Strong, Eventual, or None
Processing Transactional / Row-Column Key-value / Wide-column
History 1970s application storage 2000s unstructured storage
Scaling Product dependent Auto-spreads across commodity servers
Origin Mixture Open-source

CAP Theorem

  • Brewer's Theorem (Brewer, 2000) — developed for distributed systems
  • States a distributed system cannot comply with all parts of ACID at all times
  • "Pick Two" — at most two of three properties can exist in any shared-data system
Property Meaning
C — Consistency System operates as designed at all times
A — Availability System available when requested; responds to each request
P — Partition Tolerance System continues during data loss or partial system failure

Lambda Architecture (Ch. 14) uses CAP: Speed path (Availability + Partition Tolerance) + Batch path (Consistency + Availability)

6Database Organization

Three general ways (not mutually exclusive):

Hierarchical

  • Oldest database model; used in early mainframe DBMS
  • Most rigid structure; tree-like; mandatory parent/child (1-to-many)
  • Examples: Directory trees, XML

Relational

  • Named for relational algebra (set theory), NOT for "relation between tables"
  • Data elements (columns) related into tuples (rows); tables = sets of relations
  • Uses SQL; schema on write; row-oriented
  • DBMS = RDBMS; predominant for constantly changing data
  • Multidimensional variant — used in DW/BI; queries use MDX (Multidimensional eXpression)
  • Temporal variant — built-in time support; Valid Time + Transaction Time = bi-temporal

Non-Relational (NoSQL = "Not Only SQL")

  • Schema on read; may be row-oriented but not required
  • Goal: improved performance, especially latency and throughput
Type Key Fact
Column-oriented Compresses redundant data; suited for OLAP; BI applications
Spatial Optimized for geometric/geographic data; uses spatial index
Object/Multimedia Hierarchical Storage Management system
Flat File Single file; rows and columns; no relationships between records; Hadoop uses flat files
Key-Value Pair Document databases (XML/JSON) + Graph databases
Triplestore Subject-predicate-object (RDF); best for taxonomy, thesaurus, linked data

OLTP = row-oriented; OLAP = column-oriented

7Common Database Processes

Process Key Fact
Archiving Moving data to lower-performance media; must align with partitioning strategy; regularly test restoration
Capacity & Growth Projections Initial capacity estimate for Year 1 + growth projection for following years; includes indexes, logs, mirrors
CDC (Change Data Capture) Detects data changes; "log-based replication"; non-invasive; 2 methods: data versioning OR reading logs
Purging Completely removing data — cannot be recovered; reduces costs and risks; some data becomes liability if kept too long
Replication Same data on multiple devices; Active (every replica recreates) vs Passive (primary → secondary)
Resiliency/Recovery Immediate, Critical, Non-critical recovery types
Retention How long data kept; part of physical database design; affects capacity planning; regulatory compliance required
Sharding Small chunks updated independently; replication = file copy; refreshes/overwrites optimal

Replication Patterns:

  • Mirroring — updates replicated immediately (two-phase commit); more expensive; effective for one secondary
  • Log Shipping — secondary receives transaction logs at regular intervals; used for additional secondary servers

Replication Scaling:

  • Horizontal = more data replicas
  • Vertical = replicas geographically further apart

Active vs Passive Replication:

  • Active — recreates same data at every replica from every other replica
  • Passive — recreates on single primary, then transforms state to secondary replicas

3 Recovery Types:

  1. Immediate — resolved through design (e.g., automatic failover)
  2. Critical — restore as quickly as possible to minimize downtime
  3. Non-critical — restoration can be delayed until more critical systems restored

8Database Environments

Environment Key Facts
Production Mission-critical; business processes occur here; "real" environment
Development Slimmer version; less disk/CPU/RAM; isolated from production; first place to apply patches
Test QA, Integration Testing, UAT, Performance Testing; same hardware/software as production ideally; never writes to production
Sandbox Read-only connections to production; CRUD rights in own space; used for POC and hypotheses; should never write back to production
Alternate Production Offline backups, failover, resiliency; identical to production

9Database Availability

Availability = percentage of time a system/database can be used for productive work

4 Factors Affecting Availability (MRRS):

  1. Manageability — ability to create and maintain an environment
  2. Recoverability — ability to reestablish service after interruption
  3. Reliability — ability to deliver service at specified levels for a stated period
  4. Serviceability — ability to identify, diagnose, and repair problems

Backups:

  • Hot backup — taken while applications running; updates roll forward or roll back on reload
  • Cold backup — taken when database offline; not viable if continuous availability required
  • Backup files stored on separate filesystem, backed up to separate storage medium
  • Keep copies in secure off-site facility

10Activities

Two Main Activity Groups:

1. Manage Database Technology

  • Understand Database Technology (P)
  • Evaluate Database Technology (D) — start with POC/proof-of-concept
  • Manage and Monitor Database Technology (O) — ITIL principles apply

Technology Management Reference Model: ITIL (Information Technology Infrastructure Library) — developed in the United Kingdom

DBMS Selection Factors:

  • Product architecture, Volume/velocity limits, Application profile, Specific functionality, Hardware/OS support
  • Performance benchmarks, Scalability, Resiliency
  • Non-technical: organizational risk appetite, trained staff supply, cost of ownership, vendor reputation/support

2. Manage Databases (Database Operations)

  • Understand Requirements (P)
  • Plan for Business Continuity (P)
  • Develop Database Instances (D)
  • Manage Database Performance (C, O)
  • Manage Test Datasets (O)
  • Manage Data Migration (O)

Software Configuration Management (SCM) — 4 Procedures:

  1. Configuration Identification — identify/document/baseline all configuration attributes
  2. Configuration Change Control — processes/approval stages to change and re-baseline
  3. Configuration Status Accounting — record/report on configuration baseline at any point in time
  4. Configuration Audits — 2 types:
    • Physical — ensures installed per detailed design documentation
    • Functional — ensures performance attributes achieved

Data Migration

  • Definition: Transferring data between storage types, formats, or computer systems with minimal change
  • 5 Phases: Design → Extraction → Remediation → Load → Verification
  • Phases commonly repeated several times for moderate-to-high complexity
  • Automated and manual data remediation commonly performed during migration

Performance Issues — Common Causes:

  1. Memory allocation or contention
  2. Locking and blocking (deadlock)
  3. Inaccurate database statistics
  4. Poor coding (poorly coded SQL — most common cause)
  5. Inefficient complex table joins
  6. Insufficient indexing
  7. Application activity competing for resources
  8. Overloaded servers
  9. Database volatility
  10. Runaway queries (use query governors)

11Tools

Tool Purpose
Data Modeling Tools Automate data modeling; generate DDL; support reverse engineering; validate naming standards
Database Monitoring Tools Automate monitoring of capacity, availability, cache; alert DBAs to issues
Database Management Tools Configuration, patching, backup/restore, cloning, test management, clean-up
Developer Support Tools Visual interface for connecting to and executing commands on a database

12Techniques

  1. Test in Lower Environments — install/test on lowest level first (development), then up to production
  2. Physical Naming Standards — ISO/IEC 11179 Part 5 (Naming and Identification Principles) for naming data elements and components
  3. Script Usage for All Changes — place changes in update scripts; test in non-production first

ISO/IEC 11179 — Metadata registries (MDR); addresses semantics, representation, and registration of data descriptions

13Governance

Metrics — 4 Categories:

Category Examples
Storage Count of databases by type, capacity metrics (storage used, containers, data objects), storage service usage
Performance Transaction frequency/quantity, query performance, API service performance
Operations Data retrieval time, backup size, data quality, availability
Service Issue submission/resolution/escalation count, issue resolution time

Information Asset Tracking

  • Track and audit software license agreements and regulatory requirements
  • Yearly audits of software license costs, server leases, fixed costs
  • Out-of-compliance = serious financial and legal risks
  • Track total cost-of-ownership (TCO)

Data Audit vs. Data Validation

Concept Definition
Data Audit Evaluation of a dataset based on defined criteria; investigates specific concerns; determines if data stored in compliance with contractual/methodological requirements
Data Validation Evaluating stored data against established acceptance criteria to determine quality and usability

14Practice Q&A

Q1: What is the primary business driver for Data Storage and Operations? A: Business continuity — if systems become unavailable, operations stop.

Q2: Who coined the term ACID and when? A: Haerder and Reuter (1983). Jim Gray established the concept.

Q3: What does ACID stand for? A: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability.

Q4: What does BASE stand for? A: Basically Available, Soft State, Eventual Consistency.

Q5: What is the CAP Theorem and who proposed it? A: Brewer's Theorem (Brewer, 2000); a distributed system cannot comply with all parts of ACID at all times; must pick two of: Consistency, Availability, Partition Tolerance.

Q6: What are the 4 DBA specialization types? A: Production, Application, Procedural, Development (plus NSA for storage arrays).

Q7: What type of database is a blockchain? A: A type of federated database used to securely manage financial transactions.

Q8: What is the difference between schema on write and schema on read? A: Schema on write = relational (structure must be known before writing). Schema on read = non-relational (data can be read in different ways depending on need).

Q9: What are the two replication patterns and their difference? A: Mirroring (immediate replication via two-phase commit; more expensive) vs. Log Shipping (secondary receives transaction logs at intervals; cheaper, used for additional secondaries).

Q10: What are the 4 factors affecting database availability? A: Manageability, Recoverability, Reliability, Serviceability.

Q11: What is Change Data Capture (CDC)? A: Process of detecting that data has changed and storing relevant information; also called log-based replication; non-invasive; two methods: data versioning or reading logs.

Q12: What is the leading reference model for database technology management? A: ITIL (Information Technology Infrastructure Library), developed in the United Kingdom.

Q13: What are the 5 phases of data migration? A: Design, Extraction, Remediation, Load, Verification.

Q14: What are the 4 SCM procedures for database configuration management? A: Configuration Identification, Configuration Change Control, Configuration Status Accounting, Configuration Audits.

Q15: What is the difference between a data audit and data validation? A: Data audit = evaluating a dataset against defined criteria for compliance. Data validation = evaluating stored data against acceptance criteria for quality/usability.

Q16: What is sharding? A: Process where small chunks of a database are isolated and can be updated independently; replication is merely a file copy.

Q17: What is a sandbox environment? A: Alternate environment with read-only connections to production; allows experimentation; users have CRUD rights in their own space; should never write back to production.

Q18: Which workloads suit row-oriented vs. column-oriented storage? A: Row-oriented = OLTP (interactive transactions); Column-oriented = OLAP (analytical/data warehouse queries).

Q19: What is ISO/IEC 11179 Part 5? A: Naming and Identification Principles for physical databases — how to form conventions for naming data elements and their components.

Q20: What are the two types of configuration audit? A: Physical audit (installed per detailed design documentation) and Functional audit (performance attributes achieved).

15Quick Reference

Concept Key Fact
ACID coined Haerder & Reuter, 1983; Jim Gray established concept
CAP Theorem Brewer, 2000; pick two of C/A/P
ITIL UK; leading reference for technology management
DBA most established role Production / Application / Procedural / Development
Blockchain Type of federated database; hash algorithms; immutable
Schema on write Relational databases
Schema on read Non-relational (NoSQL) databases
Federated database Best for heterogeneous/distributed integration, MDM
OLTP Row-oriented
OLAP Column-oriented
Replication: Mirroring Immediate; two-phase commit
Replication: Log Shipping At intervals; for multiple secondary servers
Migration phases Design → Extraction → Remediation → Load → Verification
ISO/IEC 11179 Part 5 Physical naming standards
Availability factors Manageability, Recoverability, Reliability, Serviceability
Metric categories Storage, Performance, Operations, Service
